# Lab Guide

## How to use the simulator

Each module has the same layout. Read the module header, explore the architecture diagram, do the lab, and then take the knowledge check. Finish all four modules, then try the missions.

1. **Pick a module in the Skill Tree.** The left sidebar lists the 4 modules and 3 missions. The bar under each module shows how many of its objectives you have finished. Start with Module 1, because later modules build on the control loop.
2. **Read the module header.** The summary says what you will learn. Open "Key concepts" for the 5 facts the labs and quiz test. The "Module objectives" panel on the right lists what earns XP in this module.
3. **Explore the Dual-Plane Architecture Flow diagram.** The top band is the control plane (how config gets into NGINX). The bottom band is the data plane (how a request reaches a pod). The dashed green box is the single NIC pod. Click any node to open its inspector card on the right. Use the NGINX Open Source / NGINX Plus switch above the diagram to change how endpoint changes are applied.
4. **Read the packet colours.** Blue = a YAML/config change moving through the controller. Amber = an endpoint change that forces a reload (OSS). Cyan = a Plus API update, or a request served by v1. Purple = a request served by v2. Pink = a request routed by a header match. Red = a request rejected by an NGINX worker (429, 401, 403, 502 and so on).
5. **Do the lab in the Lab Console.** Every lab has a "How to run this lab" panel with numbered steps and what to watch. Modules 3 and 4 have more than one lab, so use the tabs in the Lab Console header to switch between them. Every action is also written to the "kubectl & controller events" log.
6. **Pass the Knowledge Check.** Answer every question and press Submit. You need 75% to pass. Each answer shows an explanation, and you can retry as often as you like.
7. **Earn XP, ranks and badges.** Each finished objective adds XP to the bar at the top. Ranks go from Lvl 1 YAML Apprentice to Lvl 5 Kubernetes Ingress Architect. Hover a badge to see what unlocks it. Progress is saved in your browser, and the ↺ button in the top-right resets it.

## Module 1: Pod Internals & Control Loop Flow

One pod, one container, three kinds of processes. Follow a `kubectl apply` from the API server through the IC process into nginx.conf, and see why NGINX Plus can scale upstreams without a reload.

**Key concepts**

- The NIC pod runs a single container holding the Ingress Controller (IC) Go process, the NGINX master process and the NGINX worker processes.
- Informers watch the Kubernetes API and keep a local cache. Changes are added to the Workqueue, and the Controller sync handler processes them one at a time.
- The Configurator turns resources into NGINX config using Go templates. The Manager writes files under /etc/nginx/ and asks the NGINX master to reload.
- A reload starts new workers with the new config. Old workers finish in-flight requests and then exit (worker-shutdown-timeout).
- With NGINX Plus, changes to Service endpoints are pushed through the NGINX Plus API into upstream zones, with no reload.

**Objectives (XP)**

- Inspect 4 control-plane components (+30 XP)
- Trace a kubectl apply through the control loop (+40 XP)
- Scale endpoints on NGINX OSS (observe reload) (+40 XP)
- Scale endpoints on NGINX Plus (zero reload) (+50 XP)
- Pass the Control Loop knowledge check (+60 XP)

### Lab: Control Loop Console

**Goal:** See how a kubectl apply becomes NGINX config, and why scaling pods reloads NGINX Open Source but not NGINX Plus.

**Steps**

1. Click 4 different nodes in the diagram (for example Workqueue, Configurator, NGINX Master and Worker #1) and read each inspector card. This completes "Inspect 4 control-plane components".
2. Make sure the diagram switch is set to "NGINX Open Source".
3. Press "kubectl apply -f cafe-vs.yaml". A blue YAML packet travels Developer → API Server → Informers → Workqueue → Configurator → Manager → conf.d → NGINX Master. Each node pulses as the packet reaches it.
4. When the packet reaches the master, it pulses amber (RELOADING), the worker generation number goes up, and an amber "old worker generation draining" box appears above the workers for a few seconds.
5. In part 2, press "Scale up". An amber endpoint packet follows the same path, and the compiled config on the right gets a new "server 10.244.x.x" line. The changed text is why OSS has to reload.
6. Switch the diagram to "NGINX Plus" and press "Scale up" again. This time a cyan packet goes Manager → NGINX Plus API → workers. The Reloads counter stays the same, Plus API updates goes up, and the config on the right shows a "state" file instead of server lines.

**What to watch**

- Reloads vs Plus API updates counters under the scale buttons
- "Worker gen" increases only on reload
- The events log lines from Informer, Configurator, Manager and NGINX master

> **Key takeaway:** All config changes go through the same controller pipeline. With OSS, endpoint changes also rewrite the upstream and reload NGINX. With Plus, they are patched in memory.

## Module 2: Advanced L7 Routing with CRDs

Move from annotation-heavy Ingress to typed VirtualServer resources. Split canary traffic by weight, route beta users by header, and delegate paths to other namespaces with VirtualServerRoute.

**Key concepts**

- A standard Ingress only has host and path rules. Anything more needs annotations, which are untyped strings.
- A VirtualServer is a typed CRD that holds upstreams, routes, splits, matches, actions, errorPages and snippets, and it is validated when you apply it.
- splits render as an NGINX split_clients block keyed on $request_id. The weights must add up to 100.
- matches render as map blocks on request variables, such as $http_x_beta_user. The first match that fits wins, and otherwise the route falls back to its default action or splits.
- A VirtualServerRoute lets a team in another namespace own a subtree of paths, delegated from the VirtualServer with route: <namespace>/<name>.

**Objectives (XP)**

- Edit the VirtualServer and recompile nginx.conf (+40 XP)
- Run a weighted canary split (v2 between 1% and 50%) (+50 XP)
- Route X-Beta-User traffic to v2 with matches (+50 XP)
- Explore cross-namespace VirtualServerRoute delegation (+30 XP)
- Pass the L7 Routing knowledge check (+60 XP)

### Lab: VirtualServer Canary Lab

**Goal:** Write a VirtualServer that sends a weighted share of traffic to v2, sends beta users to v2 by header, and see the NGINX config it compiles to.

**Steps**

1. Read the YAML on the left. It has two upstreams (coffee-v1, coffee-v2) and one route, /coffee, with splits of 100/0. The green bar under the editor means the IC would accept it (State: Valid).
2. Drag the Canary traffic slider to v2 10%. The YAML weights update and the compiled config on the right shows a split_clients block with 90% / 10%. You can also type in the editor directly. Try making the weights add up to 95 to see the IC validation warning, then fix it.
3. Press "kubectl apply". Your edits only reach traffic after this step, the same way a real cluster works. Wait for the blue packet to reach the NGINX master.
4. In the Traffic generator, choose 50 and press "curl × 50". The cyan (v1) and purple (v2) packets travel through the workers, and the counters show roughly 90% / 10%.
5. Turn on "matches: X-Beta-User = true → v2" and press kubectl apply again. The config gains a map $http_x_beta_user block and an @matches location.
6. Turn on the -H "X-Beta-User: true" toggle and fire again. Every request now goes to v2 by the header match and shows pink.
7. Optional: use the pod +/- buttons to scale v2 to 0 and fire. Requests sent to v2 fail with 502 because the upstream has no endpoints.
8. Press "Show VirtualServerRoute" to see how /tea is delegated to a team in another namespace.

**What to watch**

- The split_clients and map blocks in the compiled config preview
- The share of requests on the v1 and v2 bars
- The "Live:" text, which shows the config that is actually applied

> **Key takeaway:** splits become split_clients keyed on $request_id, and matches become map blocks on request variables. The IC validates the CRD before it touches NGINX, so a bad manifest never breaks live traffic.

## Module 3: Security Policies & L4 Load Balancing

Attach Policy CRDs for rate limiting, JWT, OIDC, mTLS, access control and F5 WAF to VirtualServers. Then open TCP/UDP listeners with GlobalConfiguration and route them with TransportServer.

**Key concepts**

- A Policy is its own resource, referenced from spec.policies (the server) or routes[].policies (a location) of a VirtualServer or VirtualServerRoute.
- rateLimit renders limit_req_zone and limit_req. The default rejectCode is 503, so set rejectCode: 429 to return Too Many Requests.
- jwt validates tokens at the worker (NGINX Plus). oidc runs the full authorization code flow (NGINX Plus). ingressMTLS checks client certificates. accessControl allows or denies CIDRs.
- The waf policy turns on F5 WAF for NGINX (formerly NGINX App Protect) with an APPolicy and security logging.
- GlobalConfiguration defines extra listeners (port and protocol). A TransportServer binds to one and load balances TCP/UDP in the stream context. tls-passthrough is a built-in listener.

**Objectives (XP)**

- Fire a 100-request burst into a rateLimit policy (+50 XP)
- Block tokenless requests with a jwt policy (+40 XP)
- Try ACL, mTLS or WAF enforcement (+30 XP)
- Bind a TransportServer to a GlobalConfiguration listener (+50 XP)
- Pass the Policies & L4 knowledge check (+60 XP)

### Lab: Policy Enforcement Lab

**Goal:** Attach Policy CRDs to a VirtualServer and watch the NGINX workers enforce them on a burst of 100 requests.

**Steps**

1. rateLimit starts on with rate 10r/s, burst 0 and rejectCode 503 (the NIC default). Press "Fire burst · 100 requests in 2s".
2. Watch the 10×10 grid fill in. Green squares are 200 OK and amber squares were rejected by limit_req. With 10r/s over 2 seconds, only about 20 requests get through.
3. Set burst to 20 and fire again. About 40 now pass, because the burst queue absorbs the spike.
4. Change rejectCode to 429 and fire. The rejections now read "429 Too Many Requests", and the YAML and the compiled limit_req_status line change too.
5. Turn on jwt (NGINX Plus) and set "requests with valid JWT" to 70%. Fire again. Some requests that passed the rate limit now fail with 401.
6. Try accessControl, ingressMTLS and waf one at a time. Each adds its own rejection colour, and you can see its directives (allow/deny, ssl_verify_client, app_protect_*) in the compiled config.

**What to watch**

- The order of checks: mTLS during the TLS handshake, then limit_req, then allow/deny and auth_jwt, then WAF
- Red packets stop at the workers and never reach the Service or pods
- The generated Policy YAML and the policies: list on the VirtualServer

> **Key takeaway:** Policies are separate resources that you reference from a VirtualServer or a route. They compile to NGINX directives, so they are enforced per request by the workers and the controller is never on the request path.

### Lab: TransportServer L4 Lab

**Goal:** Open a UDP port with GlobalConfiguration and route DNS traffic to it with a TransportServer.

**Steps**

1. Read the two documents in the editor. GlobalConfiguration defines the listeners dns-udp (5353/UDP) and postgres-tcp (5432/TCP). The TransportServer below it refers to a listener called dns-tcp.
2. The amber validation box says the listener "dns-tcp" is not defined. That is the bug to fix. The compiled stream config shows an ERROR line.
3. Change the TransportServer listener name to dns-udp. The warning turns green and the compiled config shows "listen 5353 udp;".
4. Optional: change protocol to TCP to see the protocol mismatch error, then change it back to UDP.
5. Press "kubectl apply", wait for the control loop to finish, then press "Send L4 traffic". Amber packets go through the workers to the pods.

**What to watch**

- The listen line and proxy_pass in the stream { } config
- The validation messages, which match what the IC reports on the TransportServer status

> **Key takeaway:** L4 ports are declared once in GlobalConfiguration (passed to the IC with -global-configuration), and each TransportServer claims one listener by name and protocol. Remember to expose the port on the NIC Service as well.

## Module 4: Production Operations & Observability

Keep NGINX stable at scale: avoid reload storms, watch the right Prometheus and OpenTelemetry signals, use the NGINX Plus live dashboard, and migrate community ingress-nginx annotations to NIC CRDs.

**Key concepts**

- Each reload starts a new set of workers while old ones drain. Many reloads close together stack up worker generations and memory, which can lead to OOMKills.
- The IC batches work: on startup and when many resources change together, it processes them as one batch and reloads once. With NGINX Plus, endpoint churn needs no reload at all.
- Prometheus (-enable-prometheus-metrics, port 9113) exposes signals such as nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_reloads_total, nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_last_reload_milliseconds and workqueue depth.
- OpenTelemetry tracing is set in the ConfigMap (otel-exporter-endpoint, otel-service-name, otel-trace-in-http). The NGINX Plus dashboard (port 8080, /dashboard.html) shows live zone and upstream health.
- Migrating from community ingress-nginx (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/*) means mapping annotations to VirtualServer fields, Policy resources, ConfigMap keys or nginx.org/* annotations.

**Objectives (XP)**

- Trigger a reload storm without batching (+40 XP)
- Survive the same churn with batching or NGINX Plus (+50 XP)
- Query reload metrics in the Prometheus console (+30 XP)
- Migrate 6 ingress-nginx annotations to NIC (+60 XP)
- Pass the Production Ops knowledge check (+60 XP)

### Lab: Reload Storm Simulator

**Goal:** Reproduce a reload storm that OOMKills the NIC pod, then remove it with batching and NGINX Plus.

**Steps**

1. Leave every protection off: Batch updates off, NGINX Plus off, worker-shutdown-timeout unset. Press "Run 60s churn".
2. Watch the memory line. Each reload (amber tick at the bottom) adds a worker generation of about 60 MiB that has not drained yet. The line climbs past the red 512 MiB limit, and a skull marks each OOMKill and restart.
3. Turn on "Batch updates" and run again. The 30 CI applies collapse into about 2 reloads, but the HPA endpoint flapping still reloads every few seconds.
4. Set worker-shutdown-timeout to 10s and run again. Old workers are cut off sooner, so memory stays under the limit, but there are still many reloads.
5. Turn on "NGINX Plus dynamic upstreams" as well and run again. Endpoint changes become Plus API updates (cyan dots) with no reload, so the run ends with about 2 reloads and a flat memory line.

**What to watch**

- Reloads, Plus API updates, Memory and OOMKills counters
- Amber reload ticks vs cyan API dots on the chart
- The verdict message under the chart

> **Key takeaway:** Reloads cost memory until old workers drain. Batching fixes bursts of config changes, NGINX Plus fixes endpoint churn, and worker-shutdown-timeout caps how long old workers can hold memory.

### Lab: Observability Console

**Goal:** Find the metrics that show reload health and see what NGINX Plus adds.

**Steps**

1. Press "Execute" to run nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_reloads_total. The result is split by reason (endpoints or other).
2. Click the suggestion chips to try the other queries: the rate() of reloads, last reload time, reload errors and workqueue depth.
3. Go to the Reload Storm tab, run a churn, then come back and query again. The reload counter now reflects that run.
4. Read the OpenTelemetry & metrics wiring box. It shows the ConfigMap keys and Deployment arguments that turn these metrics and traces on.
5. Switch the diagram to NGINX Plus to open the live dashboard mock. Scale pods in another lab and the "servers" column changes with no reload.

**What to watch**

- reloads_total split by reason
- The alert example under the console
- Upstream server counts in the Plus dashboard

> **Key takeaway:** Alert on the reload rate and on reload errors. With Plus, the dashboard and API show live upstream health per zone.

### Lab: ingress-nginx Migration

**Goal:** Translate community ingress-nginx annotations into F5 NIC resources.

**Steps**

1. Each card shows a nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/* annotation from the community controller.
2. Choose its NIC equivalent from the dropdown. A correct answer turns the card green and shows the matching NIC YAML. A wrong answer turns it red, and you can choose again.
3. Get at least 6 of the 8 right to complete the objective.

**What to watch**

- Which annotations become Policy resources and which become VirtualServer fields

> **Key takeaway:** Security features (rate limits, IP allow lists, mTLS) become Policy resources. Routing behaviour (canary, rewrite, gRPC, TLS redirect, body size) becomes VirtualServer fields.

## Missions

### Mission 1: Zero-Downtime Canary (+150 XP)

The cafe team shipped coffee v2. Its Deployment is at 0 replicas. Roll it out to internal beta users first, then to 10% of everyone, then promote it to 100%, all without a single failed request.

**Objectives**

- [ ] Scale coffee-v2 to at least 2 ready pods before sending it traffic
- [ ] Send X-Beta-User: true requests to v2 using a matches rule
- [ ] Serve 10% of general traffic from v2 (90/10 split) and fire at least 50 requests
- [ ] Promote to 100% v2 and fire at least 20 more requests
- [ ] Keep failed requests at 0 throughout

**Walkthrough**

1. v2 starts with 0 pods. Press the + next to "v2=" in the Traffic generator twice so v2 has 2 pods. If you send traffic to v2 before this, requests fail with 502 and the mission fails. Use Restart to try again.
2. Turn on "matches: X-Beta-User = true → v2", drag the slider to v2 10%, and press kubectl apply. Wait for the packet to reach the NGINX master.
3. Turn on the -H "X-Beta-User: true" toggle, choose 10, and press curl. The pink packets show beta users reaching v2.
4. Turn the header toggle off, choose 50, and press curl. That is your 90/10 canary (at least 50 requests).
5. Drag the slider to v2 100% and press kubectl apply. Then press curl again with at least 20 requests.

> **Tip:** Edits do nothing until you apply them. The progress line under the briefing counts your canary and promotion requests.

### Mission 2: Shield the Checkout API (+150 XP)

A scraper is hammering /checkout. Attach a rateLimit Policy that returns 429 (not the default 503), hold the rate at 10r/s with a burst of 20, and require a valid JWT so anonymous bots get 401.

**Objectives**

- [ ] Attach a rateLimit policy with rate 10r/s and burst 20
- [ ] Set rejectCode to 429
- [ ] Attach a jwt policy too
- [ ] Fire a 100-request burst and see both 401s and 429s rejected at the worker

**Walkthrough**

1. Turn on rateLimit. Leave rate at 10 and set burst to 20.
2. Set rejectCode to 429.
3. Turn on jwt.
4. Press "Fire burst · 100 requests in 2s". You should see 429 squares (over the limit) and 401 squares (no valid token) in the grid.

> **Tip:** The burst only counts if all three settings are in place when you fire. If an objective stays grey, check the settings and fire again.

### Mission 3: Tame the Reload Storm (+150 XP)

An HPA is flapping a 50-pod Deployment while CI applies 30 VirtualServers. The NIC pod has a 512 MiB memory limit and is getting OOMKilled. Bring reloads down and keep memory under the limit.

**Objectives**

- [ ] Reproduce the storm: run the churn with no protections and watch memory pass 512 MiB
- [ ] Run the churn again with batching and/or NGINX Plus enabled
- [ ] Finish the run with 5 reloads or fewer
- [ ] Keep peak memory under 512 MiB

**Walkthrough**

1. Run the 60s churn once with every protection off. Memory passes 512 MiB and the pod is OOMKilled.
2. Turn on "Batch updates" and "NGINX Plus dynamic upstreams".
3. Run the churn again. It should end with 5 reloads or fewer and memory under 512 MiB.

> **Tip:** Batching alone still reloads for every endpoint flap, and Plus alone still reloads 30 times for the CI burst. You need both.
